attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to code the first wave of the tower defense game in the first Build activity?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to code enemies to move automatically at certain time intervals for the first wave of the tower defense game in the first Build activity?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 If a ninja is unfamiliar with a tower defense style of game, guide them through the basic features. The user will set up towers throughout the game area. Once towers have been placed, the wave will begin where enemies will move across the screen. The towers will send projectiles towards the enemies. The user’s score increases for each enemy destroyed, but decreases if there are enemies that are able to progress through the path at the end of each wave. Each wave gets progressively faster and more challenging as more enemies appear on screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to code the first wave of the tower defense game in this first Build activity. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the tower defense code.
steps.instructions:
Welcome to Red Belt Level 2!


This is the first of 4 Build activities where you will create a tower defense project! Tower Defense is a genre of strategy games where the goal is to defend a player's territories or possessions Enemies appear in timed intervals called “waves” to attack the defenses and the tower.


Each Build activity will build off the previous activity’s code to create one complete project by the end of the level. 


In the first Build activity, you will code the first wave of the tower defense game. You’ll use the Tile Util and Sprite Utils extensions to access advanced sprite and tilemap functions to set up the first wave of the tower defense game. 


How might Tower sprites be placed on the tilemap and know where to send projectiles?

steps.hints: ❓Did you notice similarities between some of the assets, such as the different colored crab images and animations, and the different sizes of the sandcastle towers?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What might the different colored crab images and animations be used for in the tower defense project?

❓What might the different sized sand castle towers be used for in the tower defense project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice the different assets in My Assets and consider how they will be incorporated into the first wave of the tower defense project.

💡 In this project, sandcastle towers will be used to shoot projectiles at the moving crabs. Sandcastle towers will have different amounts of power, depending on their size. Each color crab will need to be hit by varying amounts of projectiles, depending on its color.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the variety of assets already in My Assets.


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and notice the different types of assets that will be used in this project, including images and their corresponding animations, and tilemaps made up of customized tiles. Only some of these assets will be used in Build 1; the rest will be used in Builds 2-4.


Why might there be different sized tower images? What might the different colored crab images be used for?

steps.hints: ❓Did you display the easyLevel tilemap asset on screen? The other tilemaps will be used in the more advanced levels later on; use easyLevel to make it easier to test this game now.
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice in the easyLevel tilemap asset?

❓ Why might a specific tile be used to indicate the end of the enemies’ path in the tower defense project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the easyLevel tilemap will make it easier to test and debug the project; the other level tilemaps will be used once the basic mechanics have been set.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice the different tiles used on the easyLevel tilemap and consider what role they will play in the tower defense project.
steps.instructions:
Display the first level’s tilemap on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // run game comment with code to set the current tilemap to the easyLevel tilemap asset underneath. 


Notice the red placeholder tile on the right side of the tilemap. That tile represents the end of the enemies’ path, but needs to be covered with the pathEndImage. 


Above // run game, add a // game initialization comment at the top of the editor. Underneath, define a coverTiles function that will be used to cover this and other tiles on the different tilemaps used in this project.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the SpriteKind namespace to declare a new PathEnd sprite kind?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the createSpritesOnTiles function do?

❓ What keywords should be used to declare a new sprite kind? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The createSpritesOnTiles function creates a sprite (with the provided image and kind) on a specific tile on the current tilemap. In this project, this function will be useful for placing the same sprite image on the endTile asset across 3 different tilemaps, where the placement of the tile differs.

💡 Remind the ninja to use namespace SpriteKind { } to create a section of code to declare new sprite kinds, the keywords export and let, the name of the sprite kind, an assignment operator, and the SpriteKind.create() function to create new sprite kinds inside the namespace block statement.
steps.instructions:
Place a sprite image on top of the red tile!


Add the arcade-tile-util extension to the project. From Tile Util, drag [on each (tile) create sprite with (image) and (kind)] into the coverTiles function definition. 


The createSpritesOnTiles function takes 3 parameters: tile, sprite image, and sprite kind. The function creates a sprite (with the provided image and kind) on a specific tile on the current tilemap. 


Update the tile parameter with the endTile asset, and the sprite image parameter with the pathEndImage asset. Create a new PathEnd sprite kind, then use that as the sprite kind parameter.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the coverTiles function after setting the current tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the coverAllTiles function do?

❓ What happens when the coverTiles function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The coverAllTiles function covers any instance of a specific tile image on the tilemap with a new tile. This allows the red placeholder tile to be covered once it has completed its purpose (placing a sprite on the end tile).
steps.instructions:
Use the function to cover the red placeholder tile after the PathEnd sprite is created.


From Tile Util, drag [cover all (tileKind) tiles with (cover)] into the coverTiles function definition. 


The coverAllTiles function will change the appearance of a tile, but will not change how a sprite reacts to the original tile “under” the cover. 


The coverAllTiles function takes 2 parameters: tile (to be covered) and cover image. Update the two tile image parameters to cover the endTile with the sandTileCover asset.


Call the coverTiles function under // run game then click ▶ to see the tilemap appear with the red tiles covered by a sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the format let array: Image[] = [] to create an empty array that will later hold image assets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the 3 variables and empty array be used for in the tower defense project?

❓ What syntax is used to declare an empty array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what happens at the start of a wave in a tower defense game. The user will place towers in various places and then when the wave begins, Enemy sprites will gradually move across the screen. The towers will fire projectiles at the Enemy sprites and the wave will end once the Enemy sprites have been destroyed or have made it to the end of the path.

💡 The 3 variables and empty array will keep track of whether the wave has started, how many Enemy sprites have appeared in the wave, and how many total Enemy sprites will be in the wave. This will be useful for triggering sprite movement, the end of wave sequence, and the user’s score.

💡 Remind the ninja to use let array: Image[] = [] to create an empty array, so that the code looks like:

let enemyImages: Image[] = []
steps.instructions:
Initialize the variables that will be used to control Enemy sprites in each wave.


Above the coverTiles function definition under // game initialization, declare a gameWave variable set to false, an enemyCount variable set to 0, an enemyNum variable set to 0, and an enemyImages empty image array.


Under the coverTiles function definition, add a // game wave functions and events comment, and create a startWave function with a waveNum number parameter underneath. Inside the function definition, set gameWave to true, enemyCount to 0, and enemyNum to the length of the enemyImages array.


These variables will keep track of whether the wave has started, how many Enemy sprites have appeared in the wave, and how many total Enemy sprites will be in the wave.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the enemyNum variable after the spawnEnemy function added images to the enemyImages array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to access the unshift array function, in order to pass the image from the spawnEnemy function’s image parameter to the enemyImages array?

❓ What will happen when the spawnEnemy function is called?

❓ Why does the spawnEnemy function need to be called before updating the value of the enemyNum variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to recall the syntax needed to access the unshift array function. They should begin by typing the array name enemyImages, then using a dot operator to access unshift. The image parameter name should be added inside of the parentheses to pass the image to the enemyImages array.

💡For simplicity in Build 1, only the red crab image will be used for the Enemy sprite. In later Build activities, additional colored crab images and animations will be added to increase the number of projectiles needed to destroy the Enemy sprites as they move across the path.

💡Because the spawnEnemy function updates the length of the enemyImages array each time a new sprite is created, the function needs to be called before the enemyNum variable is updated, to ensure the length of the array is accurate.
steps.instructions:
Define a function that will create an array of images to spawn Enemy sprites.


Under // game wave functions and events , after the startWave function definition, create a spawnEnemy function with two parameters: an image and a number. Inside the function definition, use a for loop set to count up from 0 while the counter variable is less than the number parameter. Inside the for loop, use the unshift array function to add the image passed to the image parameter to the beginning of the enemyImages array.


Call the spawnEnemy function inside the startWave function definition, above the line of code that updates the enemyNum. Pass the arguments redCrabImage as the image asset, and waveNum, the startWave function parameter, multiplied by 3, as the number.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the removeAt array function to access the last image in the array, using length - 1 to find the index of that last image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the startWave function is called?

❓ What might the period and frameInterval parameters be set to in the onUpdateInterval loop and runImageAnimation functions be set to adjust the speed and animation speed of the Enemy sprites?

❓ Did you delete let from the sprites.create function, since the Enemy sprite is already declared at the start of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the startWave function Enemy sprites will be spawned through the spawnEnemy function and onUpdateInterval loop, while the enemyCount is less than enemyNum. The ninja will be able to see 3 Enemy sprites moving across the screen (waveNum == 1, 1 * 3 = 3). Prompt the ninja to identify the number of Enemy sprites that will be spawned in wave 2.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the code and describe what they see. Prompt the ninja to tinker with the period and frameInterval parameters in the onUpdateInterval loop and runImageAnimation functions to adjust the speed and animation speed of the Enemy sprites.

💡 The section of code under // run game should be at the very end of all of the code so far, otherwise the logic of the code will not run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Spawn a wave of Enemy sprites that move across the screen, one at a time.


Add a // sprite initialization comment above // game initialization , and underneath declare an enemySprite variable using the variable name, a colon :, the variable type Sprite, and an assignment operator that sets the variable to null. This will create a global  enemySprite variable that can be accessed and updated throughout the program.


Under // game wave functions and events, after the startWave and spawnEnemy function definitions, use an onUpdateInterval loop with a conditional to spawn one new Enemy sprite every 1 second if gameWave is true and enemyCount is less than enemyNum. 


Inside the conditional, increase enemyCount by 1, then create an Enemy sprite by using and removing the last image in the enemyImages array. Open the tilemap to see the coordinates, then place the Enemy sprite on the ocean tile that aligns with the path tiles. Use the redCrabAnim asset to animate the sprite, and set its x-velocity to 40.


Last, destroy the Enemy sprite when it overlaps the endTile.  


Call the startWave function under // run game, passing 1 as the argument to the waveNum parameter. Then click ▶ to see the first wave of Enemy sprites walk along the path tiles!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create an image parameter for the createCursor function so that the cursor image can be changed later on in the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What might the Cursor sprite be used for in the tower defense project?

❓ Did you delete let from the sprites.create function, since the Cursor sprite is already declared at the start of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice the “play” button tile in the top right corner of the tilemap. The Cursor sprite will be used to interact with the play button, so that the user can determine when to start each wave.

💡 The createCursor function is needed as the Cursor sprite will change at different points in the project, and use an alternate image in later Build activities to allow the user to interact with an inventory.
steps.instructions:
Create a Cursor sprite that will give the user more control in the project.


Add a Cursor sprite kind to the project. Then, under // sprite initialization, declare a global cursor variable using the variable name, a colon :, the variable type Sprite, and an assignment operator that sets the variable to null. 


Under // game initialization, after the coverTiles function definition, define a createCursor function that takes an image as the parameter. Create a Cursor sprite inside the definition, passing the function’s image parameter. Allow the Cursor sprite to be controlled by the direction buttons, and set its z-property to a large number so that it will always appear in front of other sprites. Set two sprite flags that will allow the cursor to move through the tilemap walls while also staying in screen.


Underneath the createCursor function definition, define an initializeLevel function that will be used to set the starting conditions for each level of the project. Call the createCursor function inside the function definition, passing the arrowCursor image asset as the argument.


Last, call the initializeLevel function under the startWave function call. Then click ▶ to test the Cursor movement on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you remove the startWave code from under // run game so that the user can now control when the wave starts using the Cursor sprite and the playTile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What syntax is needed to declare a blank number variable?

❓ What will the gameWaveCount variable be used for in the tower defense project?

❓ What happens when the Cursor sprite overlaps the Play tile and the A button is pressed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use let variable: variableType = null to create an empty array, so that the code looks like:

let gameWaveCount: number = null

💡 The gameWaveCount variable will keep track of the current wave number. This is important for identifying how many Enemy sprites will appear in each wave and when the level will end.

💡 When the Cursor sprite overlaps the Play tile and the A button is pressed, the tile image will be updated, the wave count will increase and the wave will begin by spawning Enemy sprites.
steps.instructions:
Start each game wave using the Cursor sprite and the Play tile!


Under // game wave functions and events, after the onUpdateInterval loop, use an onOverlapTile function to trigger a game wave to begin when the Cursor sprite overlaps the playTile asset. Use a conditional to check if the A button is pressed, then destroy the sprite and change the playTile to the runningTile to prevent it from being pressed again until the wave ends.


Under // game initialization, declare a global gameWaveCount number variable set to null. Then, set gameWaveCount to 0 inside the initializeLevel function definition.  


Inside the onOverlapTile function, increase gameWaveCount by 1, then call the startWave function passing gameWaveCount as the argument.


Remove the startWave(1) function call from // run game. Then click ▶ to use the Cursor sprite to call a wave of Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you check that  enemyCount and enemyNum are equal, and that allOfKind().length is equal to 0? Otherwise, the game wave might not end, or end at the incorrect time.
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do the number of Enemy sprites increase in each subsequent wave?

❓ What conditions need to be true in order for the endWave function to be called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to identify the code that increases the number of Enemy sprites in each wave, which can be found in the spawnEnemy function call of the startWave function definition.  Encourage the ninja to consider why it’s important for the number of Enemy sprites to increase after each wave in the tower defense game, and how it might affect game play. 

💡 Make sure that the ninja has coded the nested conditionals inside the onUpdate loop correctly. The conditional that checks if both enemyCount and enemyNum are equal and the length of the array of Enemy sprites is 0 should be placed inside of the larger condition that checks if gameWave is true.
steps.instructions:
Create multiple waves of Enemy sprites!


Under // game wave functions and events, after the startWave and spawnEnemy function definitions, define an endWave function that will reset the game wave so that additional waves can be created. Inside, set gameWave to false and enemyImages to an empty array. Call the createCursor function, passing the arrowCursor image asset as the argument, and replace the playTile so that it can be “clicked” by the Cursor sprite again. Open the tilemap to see the coordinates for the playTile on the top right corner.


Add an onUpdate loop and call the endWave function using a nested conditional to first check if gameWave is true, and then (in the inner conditional) if both enemyCount and enemyNum are equal and the length of the array of Enemy sprites is 0.


Click ▶ then use the Cursor sprite to call multiple waves of Enemy sprites, each larger than the previous!

steps.hints: ❓Did you access the Cursor sprite’s tilemap location in the getTileLocation parameter using cursor.tilemapLocation().column and cursor.tilemapLocation().row?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which tiles can Tower sprites be placed on? Which tiles can they not be?

❓ How can you access a sprite’s tilemap location, including its column and row coordinates?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Tower sprites can only be placed on sandTile assets. This means that they cannot be placed on any of the path and ocean tiles. Additionally, once a Tower sprite is placed, the sandTile is replaced, so that another Tower sprite cannot be placed on top of it.

💡 For simplicity, only the medium tower will be used in Build 1. In later Build activities, small and large towers will be added to adjust game play. Each tower size will have different amounts of power.

💡 Remind the ninja that they need to use the tilemapLocation() function to access the Cursor sprite’s current tilemap position in both placeOnTile and setTileAt functions.
steps.instructions:
Place sandcastle Tower sprites to protect the beach from the Enemy sprites!


Add a Tower sprite kind. Then, under // sprite initialization, declare a global towerClone sprite variable set to null. 


Scroll to the bottom of all the existing code. After the code under // run game, add a // game play events comment with an A button pressed event underneath. Use a conditional to check that the tile at the center of the Cursor sprite is a sandTile, and if so, create a Tower sprite using the medTowerImage asset. Use the placeOnTile function to set the Tower sprite on the tile at the column and row location of the Cursor sprite.


Then, use the setTileAt function to replace the tile with a sandTileCover asset so that another Tower sprite cannot be placed on that tile. 


Click ▶ to test the placement of Tower sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an underscore _ to access the “hidden” pickRandom function after the getSpritesWithin function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How should the arcade-sprite-util extension be added to the project?

❓ What do the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval and getSpritesWithin functions do? How might they be used in the tower defense project?

❓ Why is an underscore _ needed to access the pickRandom function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through adding the arcade-sprite-util extension to their project. The extension was created by a member of the MakeCode Arcade development team, but has not made it into the official library yet. Prompt the ninja to type the following link into the Extensions search bar, in order to add the extension to the project:

https://github.com/jwunderl/arcade-sprite-util 

💡 The onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function makes something happen to all sprites of a certain kind at the provided interval. The getSpritesWithin function retrieves all sprites of a certain kind within a certain distance from a specific sprite. This function returns an array of sprites.

💡 _pickRandom() starts with an underscore because it is technically hidden in the JS code menu. Prompt the ninja to remember the corresponding block [pick random] in the blocks editor to select a random value.
steps.instructions:
Set the Tower sprite’s target to aim Projectiles towards the Enemy sprites that appear within a certain distance!


Under // sprite initialization, declare a global target sprite variable set to null. 


Add the arcade-sprite-util extension to the project. Open the Extensions menu, then copy and paste the following link in the search bar to add the extension to the project: 

https://github.com/jwunderl/arcade-sprite-util 


Scroll down to the bottom of all the existing code. From Sprite Utils, drag [run code on (sprite) of (kind) update every (500) ms] under // game play events, after the A button pressed event


The onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function takes 2 parameters: sprite kind and interval. Update the sprite kind parameter to Tower and the interval parameter to 1250 to make something happen for each Tower sprite every 1250 ms. 


Inside, use a conditional to check if gameWave is true. Inside the conditional, set target to any Enemy sprite that appears within a certain distance from the Tower sprite. Open Sprite Util and drag [get all sprites of (kind) within (50) pixels from (mySprite)] as the value of target .


The getSpritesWithin function takes 3 parameters: sprite kind, distance, and sprite. Update the sprite kind to Enemy, distance to 30 pixels, and sprite to the sprite variable from the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function. 


The getSpritesWithin function will return an array of sprites; to select a random sprite from that array, type a dot operator after the closing parenthesis, then _pickRandom() to pick one of the sprites at random.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Projectile’s x- and y-velocity to 0, so that they can be set by a different function in the next step?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When will target be set to true? When will it be false?

❓ What will happen if an Enemy sprite is detected within 30 pixels of the target?

❓ Why is the towerVelocity variable set in this function?

❓ Why is the sprite parameter set to sprite and not the Tower sprite name in the createProjectileFromSprite function?



Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The target variable will return false if no Enemy sprite is within 30 pixels of it when the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval code runs. It will return to true if an Enemy sprite is found.

💡 If an Enemy sprite is detected within 30 pixels of the target, a projectile will be sent from the Tower sprite. 

💡 For simplicity, the towerVelocity variable is assigned a starting value in Build 1. In a later Build activity, the variable’s value will be updated to change how often each tower size can shoot projectiles.

💡 Using sprite in the createProjectileFromSprite function allows the projectile to appear from any Tower sprite, not just one.
steps.instructions:
Shoot Projectiles from Tower sprites towards Enemy sprites!


Under // game initialization, declare a global towerVelocity number variable set to null.  


Under // game play events, inside the conditional in the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function, set towerVelocity to 40. This value will be updated again in later levels.


Because the target sprite might not identify an Enemy sprite within 30 pixels of a Tower sprite, use a nested conditional to check that target is true before creating a Projectile sprite. Set the Projectile image to projectileImage, and use the sprite variable from the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function to create a Projectile from any Tower sprite that has an Enemy sprite within range. Set the x- and y-velocity to 0 because the velocity will be set with a different function.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the angleFrom function as the second parameter in the setVelocityAtAngle function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do the setVelocityAtAngle and angleFrom functions do? How might they be used in the tower defense project?

❓ Are the projectile sprites sent from the Tower sprites towards the Enemy sprites as expected, when the wave starts?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The setVelocityAtAngle function sets the velocity of a given sprite to be at a given speed in the given direction. This function is used to set the Projectile’s velocity towards the Enemy sprites. The angleFrom function returns the angle between the center of two sprites in radians. This function can be passed to the setVelocityAtAngle function to identify the angle that the sprite’s speed will be directed in.

💡 Encourage the ninja to playtest the project repeatedly to ensure that the projectile movement is working as intended. Projectile sprites should be sent from the Tower sprites towards the Enemy sprites, as they move across the path tiles.
steps.instructions:
Set the angle and speed at which the Projectile will travel.


From Sprite Utils, drag [set (mySprite) velocity at (angle) (speed)] underneath the Projectile code. The setVelocityAtAngle function takes 3 parameters: target, angle, and speed. Set target to the Projectile variable and speed to the towerVelocity variable. 


Set the angle parameter to [angle from (mySprite) to (myEnemy)] from Sprite Utils. The angleFrom function takes 2 sprite parameters: a and b. Use the sprite variable from the onSpriteKindUpdateInterval function as the a sprite and target as the b sprite. The Projectile will now move from any of the Tower sprites in the direction of the Enemy sprite within a certain distance, at the towerVelocity speed.


Finally, set the Projectile sprites to move through the tilemap walls.


Press A to place Tower sprites, then click ▶ to start the wave and see Tower sprites shoot Projectiles when an Enemy sprite is within range.

steps.hints: ﻿❓Did you tinker with the velocity and interval values to change the speed and rate at which Enemy sprites and Projectiles are created and move throughout the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when Tower sprites shoot projectiles at the Enemy sprites? 

❓ What values might be adjusted to change how frequently Enemy and Projectile sprites move across the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to playtest the project repeatedly to ensure that the projectile movement is working as intended. Projectile sprites should be sent from the Tower sprites towards the Enemy sprites, as they move across the path tiles. 

💡Prompt the ninja to tinker with the velocity and interval values to change the speed and rate at which Enemy sprites and Projectiles are created and move throughout the project. Adjusting these values will make it easier or harder for the Tower sprites to destroy all of the Enemy sprites in each wave.
steps.instructions:
Destroy Enemy sprites with Projectiles!


Under // game play events, destroy both Enemy and Projectile sprites when they overlap. Include a sound effect to let the user know their Tower sprite successfully destroyed an Enemy sprite!


Then, under // game wave functions and events, in the endWave function definition, destroy all remaining Projectile sprites when the game wave ends.


Click ▶ to test the mechanics of the Tower, Projectile, and Enemy sprites. As needed, adjust the Enemy and Projectile velocity and the Tower interval to see how they change the game play!

header.name: BB Build 1 Tower Defense Starter Code

subgroups.introduction: Create the first level of a Tower Defense project!  Tower Defense is a genre of strategy games where the goal is to defend a player's territories or possessions. Enemies appear in timed intervals called “waves” to attack the defenses and the tower.

validationItems.text: Use a function to cover the red path tile on the tilemap.
Initialize game variables, then set their values in a function.
Use a function to spawn Enemy sprites.
Create a wave of Enemy sprites that move across the screen.
Use a function with an image parameter to create a Cursor. Call the function in a function that initializes the level.
Use the Cursor to start the game wave.
Create a function that will reset the game wave so another wave can be called.
Place Tower sprites at the Cursor sprite’s location when the A button is pressed.
Set the Enemy sprite target for the Tower sprite’s Projectile.
Aim the Projectiles at the Enemy sprites.
Destroy Enemy and Projectile sprites on overlap. Destroy remaining Projectile sprites at the end of the game wave.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Red Belt! In this level, you’ll apply your previous learning by creating a complex tower defense project in JavaScript across 4 different Build activities. There is no pre-assessment Quest activity for this level, so click “Start Level” to begin! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2

badges.title: Tower Power!
badges.description: Create a complex tower defense project in JavaScript using sprite and tile utility extensions, and a detailed Inventory menu.
